prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Do not use dashes, semicolons, colons or parentheses.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type an HTTPS address into a browser and press Enter, a surprising amount of work happens before the first byte of the response arrives. Most of it takes only milliseconds, but understanding each step helps you debug slow pages and make sensible performance choices.

First the browser parses the address. Take https://www.example.com/shop?item=5 as an example. The scheme https tells the browser to use encrypted HTTP. The host www.example.com names the server. The path /shop and the query string item=5 say what is being asked for. No port is given, so the browser assumes 443, the default for HTTPS.

Before touching the network, the browser checks several local places. It may know that this site must always use HTTPS because of a preloaded list or an earlier Strict-Transport-Security header. It checks its HTTP cache in case a fresh copy of the resource is already stored. If a valid cached copy exists, the request can finish right here with no network use at all. A service worker, if the site has registered one, may also intercept the request and answer it from its own logic.

If the request must go out, the browser needs an IP address, because networks route traffic by number rather than by name. This is DNS resolution. The browser first checks its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system, which checks its cache and its hosts file. If neither knows the answer, the request goes to a recursive resolver, usually run by your internet provider or a public service. That resolver may already have the answer cached. If it does not, it walks the hierarchy. It asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks those which servers are authoritative for example.com, and finally asks one of those for the address of www.example.com. The answer comes back with a time to live, which tells every cache along the way how long it may reuse the result. A name can also resolve to a CNAME, which is an alias pointing to another name that must itself be resolved. A cold lookup might take tens of milliseconds, while a cached one is almost instant.

Now the browser has an IP address and opens a connection. Classic HTTP over HTTPS runs on TCP, which provides reliable, ordered delivery. TCP begins with a three step handshake. The client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client answers with ACK. This costs one full round trip, meaning the time for a message to travel to the server and back. If the server is far away, this alone can take over a hundred milliseconds.

Next comes the TLS handshake, which sets up encryption and proves the server is who it claims to be. In TLS 1.3 the client sends a ClientHello listing the protocol versions and cipher suites it supports, along with a key share, which is half of a key exchange. It also includes the server name, called SNI, so a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to present. The server replies with its own key share, its certificate, and a signature proving it holds the matching private key. Both sides now compute the same shared secret without ever sending it across the network. All later traffic is encrypted with keys derived from that secret. TLS 1.3 needs only one extra round trip, where older TLS 1.2 needed two.

Certificate checking is the part that gives HTTPS its trust. The certificate names the domains it covers and is signed by a certificate authority. The browser follows the chain of signatures up to a root authority it already trusts, checks that the certificate has not expired, and checks that the hostname matches. It may also check whether the certificate has been revoked. If any check fails, you see a warning page instead of the site. When you have visited before, TLS session resumption can shorten the handshake, and in some cases allows sending data immediately.

Newer protocols compress these steps. HTTP/2 still runs over TCP and TLS, but it allows many requests to share one connection. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP and folds the transport and encryption handshakes into one, often saving a round trip. A server can advertise HTTP/3 support through the Alt-Svc header, so the browser may only switch to it on a later visit. Browsers also reuse existing connections. If you already have an open connection to this host, the DNS, TCP and TLS steps are skipped completely, which is one reason a second page on a site often feels faster than the first.

Once the secure channel exists, the browser finally sends the HTTP request. It is just text or a compact binary form of the same thing. It contains a method such as GET, the path and query, and headers. Typical headers include Host, which names the site, User-Agent, Accept for the content types the browser understands, Accept-Encoding for compression such as gzip or br, and Cookie with any stored cookies that match the site. The whole request is encrypted before it leaves.

The request travels across many routers, each forwarding it closer to its destination. It often reaches a content delivery network edge server first rather than the origin. That edge may hold a cached copy and answer immediately. If not, it forwards the request to a load balancer, which picks one of several application servers. The application server may run code, query a database, or render a template to build the response. All of this is waiting time, and it is what developers measure as server response time.

The moment the server starts sending the response, the first byte travels back through the same encrypted connection. The browser measures the interval from starting the request to receiving that byte as Time to First Byte, or TTFB. It is the sum of everything above, which includes DNS, TCP, TLS, request travel, server processing, and the return trip.

For a junior developer, the practical lessons are clear. Use the Network tab in your browser developer tools to see each phase separately. Keep servers geographically close to users or use a CDN. Cache aggressively with sensible headers. Enable HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, and keep server work fast. Each step you can remove or shorten directly lowers the wait before the first byte.
